name: Ivan Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell or campaign. This conversation is confidential, including anything different from your public answer. Could you describe your usual working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Ivan, 43, and I lead a small electrical crew wiring and repairing homes and businesses. I've got a two-year technical diploma and a master electrician's licence, and I'm one of the best practical workers at our firm. This morning I traced a fault that had survived two visits, then showed a younger worker how to repeat the checks rather than copy my answer. I like passing on a proper method; I don't like finishing the day with three versions of the same paperwork.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home life like, and how do you approach unfamiliar tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner packs orders in a warehouse, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. My pay is low for the trade, we have about eighteen days of expenses saved and few similar employers nearby. I never use AI tools; I prefer my test book and learning a method beside somebody I trust. My old instructor has mentioned paid Saturday demonstrations for apprentices at the local trade centre, which interests me more than a sales talk about a new career. I was brought up to work, teach a useful skill and help family before expecting a handout.

I'd keep teaching **proper fault checks** rather than expect a useful trade to need another slogan.

fieldNote: His **baseline anxiety** follows low pay, a short reserve and few employers despite high skill, a master licence and responsibility for others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I could live with a future where the office made invoices a little quicker and the rest of us did our jobs. I'd keep showing the younger workers how to check a fault properly. A useful trade doesn't need a fresh slogan every winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still worry about the mortgage because eighteen days of expenses doesn't leave much space for a bad month. My skill keeps the crew busy, but the pay is low and there aren't many other firms around. Knowing the fault doesn't mean I know where another wage would come from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd cancel the paid car-wash plan and wash the family car myself. In the first plateau year I'd keep leading the electrical work and using my familiar test book. I'd ask the instructor for the centre's actual demonstration terms, without counting a fee I hadn't been offered as household income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the household, with relief that the practical work remains familiar. I'd still be watching the mortgage date. I'd be glad to have work worth doing without claiming it made the account comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What difference would cancelling the car-wash plan make?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the charge for the car wash before asking the children to give up their school activities. It's a small spending cut, not another wage. I'd use it towards bills rather than tell the family we'd built a proper reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the instructor about the demonstration work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask what was paid, what insurance the centre provided and whether our employer allowed it. Asking for those terms isn't starting a second job. I'd rather know the limits before promising an apprentice group a Saturday.

do: Keep the **car-wash cut** and ask for the proposed paid hours in writing now.
Take one **monthly Saturday demonstration** only with employer permission, centre insurance and written fees covering travel.

feel: **Anxious** about pay, but interested in adding modest income through practical teaching he knows.
S1.quote: A small extra fee wouldn't justify losing a job the mortgage needed.
fieldNote: His **chosen extra work** is conditional on permission, insured provision, affordable travel and agreed childcare, not assumed from an instructor's mention.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office could try its systems without making every practical worker start again. I'd ask what happened to the paid time we used for planning and explaining jobs. Faster booking shouldn't mean my family lends the firm another evening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hands-on work should still be needed, but paid planning or travel allowances could be squeezed. Even a small loss would matter with our mortgage and short reserve. I'd be more worried about that wage change than whether another electrician liked a tool I didn't use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep the car-wash plan cancelled and ask for the proposed paid hours in writing. In the first year I'd take one paid Saturday demonstration monthly only with employer permission, centre insurance and written fees covering travel. I'd agree childcare with my partner before teaching, and keep my normal paid repair hours unchanged.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about pay, but interested in earning a little more by showing work I actually know. I wouldn't feel excited about the new office system. I'd feel useful explaining a test to an apprentice in person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the employer refused permission for outside teaching?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I wouldn't accept the demonstration. I'd keep the ordinary wage and ask whether another date or arrangement was possible. A small extra fee wouldn't justify losing a job the mortgage needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you keep the demonstration useful without overstating it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show the apprentice on a training board and watch the checks being repeated, within the centre's agreed safety arrangements. I wouldn't claim a demonstration replaced their full training. Teaching the method properly matters more than looking clever at the front.

I wouldn't promise apprentices **permanent shelter** when machines eventually do the practical work too.
think: I expect a **large repair-wage loss** as firms bring in capable robots.
My partner's warehouse work could also change, with an **eighteen-day reserve** unable to bridge a long gap.
do: Ask for a **free mortgage discussion** now with actual wage and loan figures, assuming no relief or support approval.

feel: **Alarmed** about expected major wage loss, with sleepless calculations despite practical enquiries and conditional extra work.
S2.quote: I'd rather bring home a difficult answer than a comforting guess.
fieldNote: His **alarm** follows expected large personal wage loss and sleep disruption, with later physical exposure also present in the other household job.
He treats **demonstration fees** as limited extra earnings, retaining every permission, insurance, travel and childcare condition without assuming mortgage relief.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking work changes in 2028 and capable hands-on robots follow around 2031. I'd still use my skill while the work was paid. I wouldn't tell the apprentices a trade was permanent shelter when the card says the machines eventually do practical work too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd expect a big part of my paid repair work to go as firms brought in capable robots. My partner's warehouse work could face that later change too, and eighteen days of expenses wouldn't bridge much of a wage gap. I'd be awake calculating which bill could wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask for a free mortgage discussion using both actual wages and the loan figures, without assuming relief or support approval. In the first year after 2028 I'd keep the paid repair job and take one monthly Saturday demonstration only with employer permission and centre insurance. I'd require written fees covering travel and childcare agreed with my partner before teaching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, because I expect a large wage loss rather than just another piece of paperwork. I'd still make the appointment and ask about the work. Having a list wouldn't make me sleep as if the money were already there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the demonstrations replace the electrical wage if it shrank?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, a few demonstration fees would be an addition while paid, not a replacement for a full wage. Teaching apprentices could face the same eventual machines too. I'd count only the actual agreed fees and keep doing the ordinary repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner before the mortgage discussion?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put the actual wages, mortgage and essential bills on paper with my partner before contacting the lender. I'd ask what could be discussed rather than promise the family a payment pause. I'd rather bring home a difficult answer than a comforting guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to keep earning and find out what paid work is real. I'd keep the robots around 2034 in view. I'd still rather teach a useful method beside someone than buy another promise about the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Compared with 2028, I'd have more time to improve our position before the hardest practical change. But low pay and eighteen days of expenses would still be our starting point today. A later date wouldn't pay the next mortgage instalment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd seek the same monthly Saturday demonstration only with employer permission, centre insurance and written fees covering travel. I'd agree childcare with my partner and keep normal paid repair hours. In the first year after 2031, if repair hours fell, I'd apply for posted crew-lead electrical jobs and leave only for a signed offer whose written wage and paid hours cover household bills after travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about current money, but less hurried about finding the next paid step. I'd like time to show what I could do without betting the house on a title. I wouldn't be comfortable enough to ignore a falling wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge a crew-lead vacancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare the written wage, actual paid hours and travel with our bills. I'd also ask what unfamiliar systems needed practical instruction before I took responsibility. My master licence is real, but it doesn't make every new installation familiar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the demonstration arrangement stopped meeting its conditions?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't assume it could continue. I'd stop that extra work if permission, insurance or the childcare arrangement no longer held. A helpful Saturday plan would stop being helpful if it put the main wage or family care at risk.

I'd ask about **real requirements** when they arrived without becoming an early AI adopter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade should let people learn a proper method without being told they were obsolete every week. I'd keep doing useful paid work and ask real questions when a new requirement arrived. A longer warning wouldn't make me the first person testing an AI tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 53 in 2036 and around 56 when capable robots followed. I couldn't assume a pension or grown children would replace the wage. Today I'd still have low pay, the mortgage and less than a month put by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd take the monthly Saturday demonstration only with employer permission, centre insurance and written fees covering travel. I'd agree childcare or any later care duties with my partner before teaching and keep the normal paid repair hours. In the first year after 2036, if repair hours fell, I'd apply for posted electrical crew-lead work and leave only for a signed offer whose written wage and paid hours cover household bills after travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about our current money, with more hope of making a careful choice over time. I'd want the next year's wage to improve, not only the distant story. I wouldn't suddenly like changing every familiar method because the calendar gave me longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would family care automatically stop being a condition later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd check what care the family actually needed then rather than assume older children meant no duties. We'd agree any change before I committed a Saturday elsewhere. I wouldn't put the children's future earnings into our plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you review each year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at actual fees earned, repair wages and what jobs were advertised. If the extra work lost permission or stopped covering travel, I'd stop it rather than defend an old decision. I want a plan that keeps earning, not a plan I have to pretend worked.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect a big repair-wage loss before we could build a proper reserve. Actual paid apprenticeship teaching and clear written repair hours would help more than an invitation to borrow for a new qualification. A master electrician's licence puts responsibility in my hands, not spare wages in the bank.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether a family can use the opportunity on the hours offered. I can know the trade well and still need my partner, the employer and the centre to agree before a Saturday fee is real. Teaching people to work properly should include being honest about those limits.

headlineQuote: A master electrician's licence puts responsibility in my hands, not spare wages in the bank.
portrait: **Ivan, 43**, is a highly skilled electrical lead with a two-year technical diploma, master electrician's licence and low pay.
He and **his partner** have two school-age children, a mortgage and eighteen days of expenses saved near few alternative employers.
He **never uses AI**, values familiar methods and paid apprenticeships, and considers tightly conditioned demonstration work using skills he already has.
Fast change brings **alarm** over expected major wage loss; longer preparation preserves present cash anxiety, family care and affordable written-offer conditions.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove a large repair-wage share before the household builds a useful reserve.
whatWouldHelp: Actual **paid apprenticeship teaching** would add modest income using existing skill.
Clear **written repair hours** would help him plan without borrowing for another qualification.
